title: Thermodynamic Limits on Reliable Signaling by Biochemical Traveling Waves
authors: Shengyao Luo, Yuping Chen, Yuansheng Cao
abstract: Biochemical traveling waves transmit signals across cells and tissues, but the thermodynamic cost of reliable propagation remains unclear. We develop a stochastic thermodynamic framework for reaction--diffusion systems with stable traveling waves and show that diffusion of the wave position is bounded by the dissipation specifically associated with propagation. The bound follows by projecting noisy field dynamics onto the adjoint translational mode, which maps the wave position to an effective biased random walk. Its tightness is controlled by the non-self-adjoint part of the linearized dynamics, with finite wave speed and antisymmetric reaction dynamics generically producing deviations from equality. For excitable trigger waves in a FitzHugh--Nagumo model, we show that the slow inhibitor dominates the propagation cost, yielding a trade-off among wave speed, inhibitor amplitude, and dissipation. We test these predictions in stochastic simulations of a microscopic Belousov--Zhabotinsky reaction--diffusion system and find consistent signatures in mitotic trigger-wave experiments in \textit{Xenopus} egg extracts. The same relation further imposes an annihilation-limited bound on the reliable signaling rate of wave trains.
summary: This work establishes a fundamental thermodynamic constraint linking noise (wave diffusion) to energy cost (dissipation) for signal propagation via biochemical waves. By developing a stochastic framework and testing it on both simulated BZ systems and live Xenopus experiments, the authors show that reliable signaling requires a minimum energetic investment proportional to wave fluctuations.
main_problem: The central goal is determining the fundamental thermodynamic cost associated with maintaining reliable signal propagation via biochemical traveling waves.
main_result: A rigorous thermodynamic bound links the wave's positional diffusion constant ($D_X$) to the dissipation rate ($\dot{W}_{	ext{prop}}$), suggesting that energy expenditure dictates noise resilience in biological signaling.
method: The authors developed a stochastic thermodynamic framework, projecting noisy field dynamics onto an adjoint translational mode to derive effective random walk statistics and calculate entropy production rates.
model_or_system: The study uses reaction-diffusion systems exhibiting excitable traveling waves, modeled by FitzHugh-Nagumo or Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) kinetics. Validation is performed using both stochastic simulations of the BZ system and live imaging of mitotic trigger waves in Xenopus egg extracts.
key_observables: Wave position diffusion constant ($D_X$), propagation dissipation rate ($\dot{W}_{	ext{prop}}$), wave speed ($c$), and inhibitor amplitude.
important_parameters: The bound itself, $D_X \dot{W}_{	ext{prop}} / c^2 \geq 1$, and the timescale separation parameter $\varepsilon$ in quasi-static approximations.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on weak noise regimes and assumes that the system can be accurately described by projecting dynamics onto a collective coordinate (the wave position).
figures_summary: Figures conceptually decompose wave fluctuations into diffusive positional modes, show schematic relationships between propagation and dissipation in FHN models, and present quantitative comparisons of $D_X/c^2$ vs $\dot{W}_{	ext{prop}}$ for both simulated BZ waves and experimental Xenopus data.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the general stochastic thermodynamic framework, derives the key bound by analyzing the adjoint translational mode, applies this to simplified models (like FHN), validates it using controlled simulations (BZ), and finally tests the predictions against complex biological systems (Xenopus).
why_interesting: While focused on biochemistry, the mathematical machinery—deriving bounds from non-equilibrium thermodynamics applied to pattern formation—is highly relevant to understanding energy dissipation in any driven, fluctuating physical system, including those studied in AMO physics.

The slow inhibitor field remains elevated over the extended refractory tail behind the waveback (with characteristic length of lm) and dominates the propagation dissipation.
